text: Only a few people of Indian birth or citizenship have been to space. The first was Rakesh Sharma, an Indian Air Force pilot who flew on a Soviet spacecraft in 1984. The second Indian citizen was Shubhanshu Shukla, also an air force pilot, who spent about 18 days on the International Space Station in 2025.

Two women born in India or to Indian families flew with NASA. [[@kalpana-chawla|Kalpana Chawla]] grew up in Karnal, Haryana, and became an American astronaut. Sunita Williams, whose father came from Gujarat, spent 608 days in space. A few Indian-born travellers have also made short trips to the edge of space on private rockets.
India is now preparing to launch its own astronauts on its own rocket. Four air force pilots have been chosen and are training for the [[@gaganyaan|Gaganyaan]] mission.

sec.t:
In the 1980s the Soviet Union invited friendly countries to send a guest astronaut to its space station. India picked two air force pilots, Rakesh Sharma and Ravish Malhotra, to train in Russia. Sharma flew, and Malhotra was his backup.

On 3 April 1984, Sharma launched with two Soviet cosmonauts from Baikonur. He spent nearly eight days aboard the space station Salyut 7. He did experiments on how the body copes with weightlessness, and took photographs of India from [[orbit|orbit]] to help map its land.

During a live TV call, Prime Minister [[@indira-gandhi|Indira Gandhi]] asked him how India looked from space. He replied, in Hindi, "saare jahan se achha", a line from a famous patriotic song. It means "better than the whole world". Many Indians still remember that moment.

Kalpana Chawla studied aeronautical engineering in Chandigarh and then in the USA, where she became a citizen. She flew on the space shuttle Columbia in 1997, the first woman born in India to go to space.

In 2003 she flew again. On the way home, Columbia broke apart as it came back through the [[atmosphere|atmosphere]], and all seven crew members died. Schools, a hostel and a satellite in India have been named after her.

Sunita Williams was born in Ohio, USA, to an Indian father and a Slovenian-American mother. She made three long stays on the space station. Her last mission, in 2024 and 2025, was meant to last about a week, but problems with her spacecraft stretched it to nine months. She retired from NASA in December 2025 after 608 days in space.

{{story:cold-war}}

In June 2025 Group Captain Shubhanshu Shukla, from Lucknow, flew to the International Space Station on a private mission called Axiom-4, launched on a SpaceX rocket from Florida. He was the mission's pilot.

He became the first Indian to visit the station and the second Indian citizen in space. Over about 18 days he ran experiments chosen by Indian scientists, including growing seeds such as methi and moong in weightlessness to see how they sprouted. He returned in July 2025, splashing down off the coast of California.

In February 2024 ISRO named four astronaut-designates for India's first crewed spaceflight: Prasanth Nair, Ajit Krishnan, Angad Pratap and Shubhanshu Shukla. All four are test pilots in the [[@indian-air-force|Indian Air Force]].

Gaganyaan aims to launch two or three astronauts on an Indian rocket from Sriharikota, keep them in orbit for up to three days and bring them safely back to the sea. First come uncrewed test flights. One of them will carry Vyommitra, a humanoid robot that sits in a crew seat and reports what a human would feel.

When the first crewed flight happens, India will become only the fourth country to send people to space on its own rocket, after Russia, the USA and China.

text: A star's colour tells you how hot its surface is. Everything that is hot enough glows, and the colour of that glow changes with temperature. Cooler stars glow red or orange. Medium ones, like our [[@sun-what|Sun]], look white or yellowish. The hottest stars glow blue.

You can see the same thing on Earth. An iron rod in a blacksmith's fire first glows dull red, then bright orange, then yellow-white as it heats up. A star is a giant ball of glowing gas, and the same rule applies. [[astronomer|Astronomers]] can look at a star's colour and work out its temperature without ever going near it.

st.reveal: Rigel's surface is around 11,000 °C, while Betelgeuse's is only around 3,300 °C. In stars, blue means hot and red means cool, just as a gas flame burns blue where it's hottest.

sec.t:
Everything gives off light, even you. At body temperature, that light is [[infrared|infrared]], which our eyes can't see but heat cameras can. Heat something to about 500 °C and it starts to glow a faint red. Keep going and the glow shifts to orange, yellow, white and finally blue-white.

The reason is that hotter objects give off more energetic light, with shorter [[wavelength|wavelengths]]. Red light has long waves. Blue light has short ones. A cool star pours out mostly red and infrared light. A very hot star pours out more blue and [[ultraviolet|ultraviolet]].

The same shift happens at home. The coil of an electric heater glows dull red when it is warm and brighter orange as it gets hotter. A gas flame burns blue at its hottest point and yellow where it is cooler and sootier.

{{story:rainbow-how}}

Red stars have surfaces of around 2,500 to 3,500 °C. That is still hot enough to melt iron, but cool for a star. The Sun's surface is about 5,500 °C. Blue giants can be 10,000 to more than 40,000 °C.

In the early 1900s, astronomers at Harvard sorted hundreds of thousands of stars by the patterns in their light. Annie Jump Cannon, who was partly deaf, could [[classify|classify]] a star in seconds, and she sorted around 350,000 in her lifetime. Her system put stars into classes O, B, A, F, G, K and M, from hottest to coolest. Students remember the order with the line "Oh Be A Fine Girl, Kiss Me" or "Oh Be A Fine Guy, Kiss Me". The Sun is a G star.

Every star shines across a whole rainbow of colours at once. Its colour is just the shade that's strongest. A star whose light peaks in the green part of the [[spectrum|spectrum]] still gives off plenty of red and blue too. The mix looks white to our eyes, which is why the Sun, whose light peaks in the blue-green, looks white from space.

So you won't see a green or purple star. Some double stars look greenish next to a strongly orange partner, but that's a trick of contrast, the way a grey square looks bluish beside a bright orange one.

Most stars look white to the naked eye. In dim light, our eyes use cells that can't see colour well. The brightest stars, though, show their colours clearly.

In the [[@constellations|constellation]] of Orion, reddish Betelgeuse marks one shoulder, and blue-white Rigel marks the opposite knee. Indian astronomers knew Betelgeuse as Ardra, one of the 27 nakshatras. Orange Aldebaran, in Taurus, is Rohini. In the summer sky, red Antares shines in Scorpius. Its Greek name means "rival of Mars" because its colour matches the red planet.

Colour also tells a star's fate. Blue stars burn through their fuel in a few million years, while small red ones can shine for far longer than the universe has existed so far. Their whole [[@star-life-cycle|life cycle]] is written partly in their colour.

text: A day on the Moon is very long, very bright and very quiet. The Moon turns slowly, so the Sun takes about two Earth weeks to cross its sky. Then comes two weeks of night.

There is no air, so the sky stays black even at noon. Stars would be faint in the glare, but the Sun would blaze white. In sunlight the ground heats to about 120°C, hotter than boiling water. At night it can fall to about −130°C. You would weigh only one-sixth of what you weigh at home, and you could not hear a single sound outside your helmet.

st.reveal: Vikram and its rover Pragyan landed in August 2023 and ran on sunlight. When the long lunar night arrived after about two Earth weeks, they were put to sleep. They never woke up in the cold that followed.

d.try: Measure a Moon jump. Jump as high as you can next to a wall and ask a friend to mark the height with a sticky note. Multiply that height by six. That is roughly how high the same jump would take you on the Moon, if your spacesuit let you bend your knees.
myth: One side of the Moon is always dark, the "dark side of the Moon".
There is a far side that we never see from Earth, but it gets just as much sunlight as the near side. When we see a new Moon, the far side is actually in full daylight.
facts: Length of one Moon day (sunrise to sunrise)

sec.t:
On Earth, the Sun rises in a couple of minutes. On the Moon, it creeps up so slowly that sunrise takes about an hour. There is no colourful dawn, because colours in the sky come from air [[@sky-blue|scattering light]]. The Sun just appears over the grey horizon like someone switched on a stadium floodlight.

Shadows are inky black and sharp. With no air to spread light around, a rock's shadow can be dark enough to hide your own boots.

The Moon's weak [[gravity|gravity]] changes everything. Apollo astronauts found walking awkward and often hopped like kangaroos instead. Dropped tools fell slowly. In 1971, Alan Shepard hit two golf balls on the Moon. His one-handed swing was poor, but the balls still sailed far.

A cricket ball thrown by a fast bowler on the Moon would fly much farther than on Earth. But you could not breathe, so every jump would happen inside a [[@spacesuits|spacesuit]] that, with its backpack, weighed about 90 kg on Earth.

Moon dust is not soft like beach sand. Without wind or water to wear it smooth, each grain stays jagged like crushed glass. It stuck to Apollo suits, scratched visors and made astronauts sneeze when they took off their helmets.

A Moon base would need thick walls or a blanket of soil on top to block heat, cold and [[radiation|radiation]] from the Sun. Some [[crater|craters]] near the poles never see sunlight at all. They are colder than −240°C and hold [[@moon-water|frozen water]] that future explorers might drink or turn into rocket fuel.

On 23 August 2023, India's [[@chandrayaan|Chandrayaan-3]] lander, Vikram, touched down near the Moon's south pole. It was timed to land just after local sunrise, so it would get a full lunar daytime of solar power. Its [[rover|rover]], Pragyan, rolled out and found sulfur in the soil.

After about 14 Earth days, sunset came and the long cold night began. Both were put to sleep, and they never woke up again.

In April 2026, NASA's Artemis II mission flew four astronauts around the Moon, the first crew to travel that far since 1972. NASA plans to land people near the south pole in the coming years. Countries including China and India have their own plans to send astronauts too.

The first people to spend a full Moon day there will have to survive two weeks of night. Planners are already looking past that, to an even harder target: building homes on [[@mars-colonies|Mars]].

text: When you land on a trampoline, the mat sinks and stretches dozens of [[@springs|springs]] around the edge. Those springs store the energy of your fall, a bit like a bow being drawn back. A split second later they snap back to their normal length and fling the mat, and you, upward.

On hard ground, most of the energy of landing is lost in your knees, the ground and the sound of your feet. A trampoline wastes much less. And if you push down with your legs just as the mat reaches its lowest point, you add new energy, so you go higher than before.

st.prompt: If you stand still on a trampoline and just let yourself drop a little, then do nothing, what happens to your bounces?

options.t: Each bounce gets a little lower until you stop
You keep bouncing at the same height forever

st.reveal: Each bounce loses a bit of energy as heat in the springs and mat and as sound. A trampoline can only give back the energy you put in. To go higher, you must push down with your legs at the bottom of every bounce.

d.try: Drop a tennis ball and a ball of clay from the same height onto a hard floor and watch which bounces higher. Then drop the tennis ball onto a pillow. Where did the "bounce energy" go in each case? A trampoline is built to give back as much energy as possible.
myth: A trampoline adds extra energy to your jump, which is why you go so high.

A trampoline cannot create energy. It stores the energy of your fall and your leg push in its springs and gives most of it back. You go higher on a trampoline mainly because it wastes less energy than the ground and gives you more time to push.

sec.t:
At the top of a bounce, you are moving slowly and are full of stored "height energy". As you fall, [[@gravity-fall|gravity]] turns that into speed. When you hit the mat, the speed turns into stretch energy in the springs. Then the springs turn it back into speed, and the speed back into height.

If nothing were lost, you would bounce to the same height forever. In real life, every bounce loses a little energy as heat and noise. So jumpers bend their knees and push hard at the bottom of each bounce, topping up the energy each time, like pushing a swing at the right moment.

sec.h: Why a trampoline beats a floor

sec.t:
In the 1930s, George Nissen was a teenage gymnast in Cedar Rapids, Iowa. He watched trapeze artists at the circus drop into safety nets and bounce back up, and thought the bounce looked more fun than the act. With his coach, Larry Griswold, he built a frame of scrap iron with canvas stretched across it.

Nissen named it after "trampolín", the Spanish word for a diving board, which he heard while touring Mexico. He sold trampolines for decades. To advertise them, he once bounced alongside a kangaroo in New York.

During the Second World War, the US Navy used trampolines to train pilots and navigators, teaching them to stay aware of which way was up while flipping in the air.

Trampoline became an [[@olympics|Olympic]] sport at the Sydney Games in 2000. Elite athletes bounce on very springy beds, reaching about 8 to 10 metres, roughly the height of a three-storey building. At the top, they have a little over two seconds in the air to fit in somersaults and twists.

Judges score the difficulty of the moves, how neatly they are done, how long the jumper spends in the air and how close they stay to the centre of the bed. Drift too far and you lose points, or worse, land on the frame.

Most trampoline injuries happen when more than one person jumps at once. A lighter child can be launched sideways when a heavier person lands at the same moment. Safety nets, padding over the springs and one jumper at a time cut the risk a lot.

Nature had the idea long before Nissen. A [[@wild-kangaroo|kangaroo's]] leg [[tendon|tendons]] stretch like springs every time it lands, storing energy and giving it back, so a hopping kangaroo uses surprisingly little effort as it speeds up.

text: Ordinary cloth is made of threads with tiny gaps between them. Water soaks into the threads and seeps through the gaps. To make cloth waterproof, you either block the gaps completely, with a coating of rubber, plastic or wax, or you make the gaps so small that liquid water can't get through.

The cleverest rain jackets do something more. They have a thin inner layer full of microscopic pores. Raindrops are far too big to pass through them, but water vapour from your sweat is small enough to escape. That is what makers mean by "breathable".

st.prompt: A breathable rain jacket keeps rain out but lets sweat escape. How can one material do both?

options.t: Its holes are too small for liquid drops but big enough for water vapour
It has a tiny fan sewn inside
It soaks up the sweat and stores it in the lining

st.reveal: Sweat leaves your skin partly as invisible water vapour, single molecules floating in the air. A breathable membrane has pores far smaller than a raindrop but larger than a water vapour molecule. Drops stay out, and vapour drifts through.

sec.t:
Long before Europe had raincoats, peoples in Central and South America collected the milky sap of rubber trees. They used it to make balls, shoes and waterproof cloth. European explorers brought rubber back as a curiosity.

In 1823, a Scottish chemist named Charles Macintosh found a way to [[dissolve|dissolve]] rubber in a liquid made from coal tar. He spread it between two layers of cloth and pressed them together. The rubber in the middle stopped water completely. Coats made from this "Macintosh" cloth became popular in rainy Britain, even though they smelled, went stiff in the cold and turned sticky in the heat.

In 1839, the American inventor Charles Goodyear found that heating rubber with sulphur made it much tougher and less sensitive to temperature. This process, called vulcanisation, made rubber raincoats, boots and tyres far better.

In the 1900s, plastics such as PVC replaced rubber in cheap raincoats. A plastic raincoat is simply a thin, flexible sheet with no holes at all. It is light and cheap, which is why so many children in India pull one on over their school uniform in the [[@monsoon|monsoon]].

The problem is sweat. Your body gives off water all the time, even when you are not running. In a plastic coat, it has nowhere to go. It condenses on the inside, and after a long walk you may feel as wet as if you had no coat at all.

In 1969, an American engineer named Bob Gore was working with a slippery plastic called PTFE, the material used on [[@non-stick-pans|non-stick pans]]. He found that stretching it quickly turned it into a thin sheet full of tiny holes. The material, called Gore-Tex, went into rain jackets in the 1970s.

Its pores are thousands of times smaller than a raindrop but hundreds of times bigger than a [[molecule|molecule]] of water vapour. Rain stays out, and the vapour from your skin slowly escapes. Many outdoor jackets now use membranes like this, sandwiched between an outer fabric and a soft lining.

Most rain jackets also have a water-repellent finish on the outside, which makes drops bead up the way they do on a [[@lotus|lotus leaf]]. Some of these finishes use chemicals that last a very long time in nature, so many companies are switching to newer, cleaner ones.

People in rainy places have always found their own answers. Farmers in Assam wear the *japi*, a wide hat woven from bamboo and palm leaves. In Kerala, some farmers working in paddy fields still use a hat-like umbrella made of palm leaf that leaves both hands free.

text: Empathy is the ability to understand and share the [[@emotions|emotions]] someone else is feeling. When your friend loses a match and your own stomach sinks, that's empathy. So is noticing that a classmate has gone quiet and guessing something is wrong at home.

Psychologists often split empathy into parts. Emotional empathy is catching some of another person's feeling, like flinching when you see someone stub their toe. Cognitive empathy is working out what someone feels and why, almost like stepping into their shoes. Compassion goes one step further, adding the wish to help. Together, these let people live, play and work alongside each other.

st.prompt: In a famous experiment, a rat could open one cage holding a trapped rat, or another holding chocolate. What did most rats do?

options.t: Freed the trapped rat, and often shared the chocolate with it
Ate all the chocolate and ignored the trapped rat
Did nothing at all

st.reveal: Most rats learned to open the trapped rat's cage, and many did so before eating. Often they left some chocolate for their freed companion. The scientists argued this was a simple form of empathy.

d.try: Watch two minutes of a film or cartoon with the sound turned off. Pause on a character's face and guess what they are feeling and why. Then turn the sound on and check. Reading faces and situations like this is a big part of cognitive empathy, and it gets better with practice.
myth: You're either born with empathy or you aren't, and it can't change.

Most people are born with the ability, but how much they use it grows with practice, experience and good examples. Listening carefully, reading stories and spending time with people different from you can all strengthen it.

understanding what they feel and why

sec.t:
Empathy starts early. Studies going back to the 1970s found that newborns in hospital cry more when they hear another baby cry. They cry less at a recording of their own crying, so it's not just noise that sets them off.

By around 18 months, toddlers start to help. In a well-known 2006 study in Germany, a grown-up dropped a clothes peg or struggled to open a cupboard while carrying books. Most toddlers waddled over to help, without being asked or rewarded. Young chimpanzees did something similar.

Over childhood, the thinking side grows. Children learn that others can have different feelings, wishes and knowledge from their own, and that a smile can hide sadness. Psychologists call this understanding "theory of mind", and most children have a good grip on it by about the age of five.

Scientists have scanned people's brains while they watched someone they love receive a mild electric shock. Some of the same areas that respond to a person's own pain lit up when they saw a partner in pain. They weren't feeling the shock, but part of the brain seemed to rehearse it.

In the 1990s, researchers in Italy found [[neuron|neurons]] in monkeys that fired both when a monkey grabbed food and when it watched someone else grab food. They were named mirror neurons. Some people claimed they explained human empathy. Most scientists now think they are only part of a more complicated story.

Empathy has limits. People tend to feel it most for those who look like them, live near them or belong to their group. One sad story about a single named child often moves people more than news about thousands who are suffering.

Some thinkers, like the psychologist Paul Bloom, argue that empathy can even lead us astray, and that calm, fair kindness is a better guide for big decisions. Others reply that without empathy we wouldn't care in the first place. Both sides agree that feeling for others is a starting point, and that [[@kindness-science|kindness]] is what turns it into action.

Empathy can get stronger. Listening without interrupting, asking "How did that feel?" and reading stories about people unlike yourself all seem to help. A Canadian programme called Roots of Empathy, started in 1996, brings a baby and parent into classrooms so children can watch the baby grow and talk about its feelings. Studies have linked it to less fighting and [[@bullying|bullying]] among students.

text: Decimals are a way of writing parts of a whole using our ordinary base-ten digits. The decimal point separates the whole number from the parts. The first digit after the point counts tenths, the next hundredths, the next thousandths, and so on.

So 3.75 means 3 wholes, 7 tenths and 5 hundredths, which is the same as three and three quarters. Decimals are easier to add, subtract and compare than [[@fractions|fractions]], which is why we use them for money, [[@maths-sport|sports times]] and measurements. Your height, your weight and the price of a [[@samosa|samosa]] can all be written as decimals.

st.prompt: Which of these numbers is the biggest?
st.reveal: 0.5 means five tenths, which is a half. 0.25 is a quarter and 0.125 is an eighth. Having more digits after the point does not make a decimal bigger. What matters is the value in each place.

myth: A decimal with more digits is always bigger, so 0.25 is more than 0.5.

Each place after the point is worth ten times less than the one before. 0.5 means 5 tenths, while 0.25 means 2 tenths and 5 hundredths. So 0.5 is bigger. Adding a zero to the end, as in 0.50, does not change the value at all.

sec.t:
In a whole number like 333, each 3 is worth ten times the one to its right: 300, 30 and 3. Decimals simply keep the pattern going past the ones place. The next 3 to the right is worth three tenths, then three hundredths, then three thousandths.

That is why 0.1 is the same as 1/10, 0.01 is 1/100 and 0.5 is 5/10, or one half. Some fractions do not fit neatly. One third becomes 0.3333..., with threes going on forever. Mathematicians write that with a little line or dot over the 3.

The United States was one of the first countries to make its money fully decimal. From 1792, a dollar was divided into 100 cents, rather than awkward fractions. That made sums much simpler for shopkeepers and banks.

India's rupee used to be split into 16 annas, each worth 4 paise. On 1 April 1957, India switched to decimal coins, with 100 naye paise, or "new paise", to the rupee. Britain followed in 1971, giving up a system where a pound had 20 shillings and each shilling 12 pennies. Today almost every [[currency|currency]] in the world is decimal.

The [[@metric-system|metric system]] is built on decimals. A metre has 100 centimetres and 1,000 millimetres, so 1.5 metres is simply 150 centimetres. A kilogram has 1,000 grams, so 0.25 kilograms is 250 grams.

In sport, decimals can decide everything. At the Tokyo Olympics, held in 2021, [[@neeraj-chopra|Neeraj Chopra]] won the javelin with a throw of 87.58 metres, India's first Olympic gold in athletics. [[@usain-bolt|Usain Bolt]]'s 100-metre world record, set in 2009, is 9.58 seconds. Races are timed to hundredths of a second, and sometimes the winner is decided by just 0.01 seconds.

Rounding decimals can cause trouble when it happens again and again. In 1982, a stock exchange in Vancouver, Canada, started a new index, a single number showing how share prices were doing. Each time it was updated, the computer chopped off the last decimal places instead of rounding properly. After about two years of thousands of updates a day, the index had lost roughly half its true value. When it was fixed, it jumped up overnight. Small digits, it turned out, can add up.

text: A box is a 3D shape, but it can start life flat. If you cut along some of a box's edges and unfold it, you get a single flat piece called a **net**. Fold the net back along the same lines and the box returns.

Every cardboard box, sweet box and cereal packet is made this way. Factories print and cut nets from big flat sheets, then fold and glue them. For a cube, the net is six squares joined edge to edge. But not just any six squares will do. Only 11 arrangements fold into a cube, and finding them all is a good puzzle.

st.reveal: You can join six squares edge to edge in 35 different ways, but only 11 of them fold up into a cube. The others leave a gap on one side and a double layer on another.

Only 11 of the 35 possible six-square shapes work. A straight row of six squares, for example, rolls into a tube with two open ends.

sec.t:
Shapes with flat faces and straight edges, like cubes and pyramids, are called [[polyhedron|polyhedra]]. A cube has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 corners. In the 1700s, the Swiss mathematician Leonhard Euler noticed a pattern: for these shapes, faces plus corners minus edges always equals 2. For a cube, 6 + 8 - 12 = 2.

That rule helps when you design a net. To unfold a cube you must cut along exactly 7 of its 12 edges, leaving 5 as folds holding the faces together. A triangle-based pyramid is simpler: it has only 2 different nets.

In 1525, the German artist Albrecht Dürer published a book about measuring and drawing. In it, he showed solid shapes unfolded flat, so readers could copy them, cut them out and fold their own models. His is one of the earliest known books to show nets this way.

Dürer's idea left a puzzle that is still open. For any shape with flat faces that bulges outward everywhere, can you always cut it along its edges into one flat net with no overlaps? It seems likely, and it works for every example tried. Yet nobody has proved it must always work.

Real boxes need more than the plain net. Packaging designers add tabs, which are thin flaps that get glued or tucked in, and they plan where the box will be weakest. A pizza box folds from one cut sheet with no glue at all, using slots and tabs. A mithai box often has a lid that is a second, slightly bigger net.

Designers also think about waste. They fit as many nets as they can onto one big sheet, a bit like fitting tiles on a floor, so less cardboard is thrown away. Once you've opened a box flat and counted its tabs, every packet in a shop starts to look like a puzzle someone has already solved.

Folding flat things into shapes isn't only for boxes. Engineers borrowed ideas from [[@origami-maths|origami]] to fold solar panels and sunshields so they fit inside rockets, then open in space. Bees, meanwhile, build their [[@honeycomb|honeycomb]] from six-sided cells that pack together with no gaps. Working out how much a box can hold is a [[@area-volume|volume]] problem, and working out how to make it from one flat sheet is a nets problem.

text: Women have done important mathematics for at least 1,600 years, often while being told they shouldn't. Many were blocked from universities, paid less or had their work credited to men. Some taught themselves from borrowed books.

A few of the best known are [[@maths-history-women|Hypatia]] in ancient Alexandria, [[@ada-lovelace|Ada Lovelace]] and Sophie Germain in the 1800s, and Emmy Noether in the early 1900s. Closer to our time come [[@moon-race-women|Katherine Johnson]] in the United States, [[@shakuntala-devi|Shakuntala Devi]] in India and Maryam Mirzakhani from Iran. Their work runs through modern physics, computing and space travel.

sec.t:
Hypatia lived in Alexandria, in Egypt, around 1,600 years ago. Her father, Theon, was a mathematician, and she became a famous teacher of maths, astronomy and [[philosophy|philosophy]]. Students travelled long distances to hear her.

She worked on editions of older Greek maths books, including works on astronomy and [[geometry|geometry]], and helped preserve them. She was killed in 415 CE during a period of violent political and religious conflict in the city. She is often remembered as the first woman mathematician whose life is well recorded.

Emmy Noether was a German mathematician who, for years, was not allowed to be paid as a university teacher because she was a woman. She lectured under a male colleague's name.

In 1918 she proved what is now called Noether's theorem. It links patterns of [[@symmetry|symmetry]] to rules in physics, such as why energy is never lost. Physicists still use it every day. After she died in 1935, [[@einstein|Albert Einstein]] wrote in a letter to *The New York Times* that she was the most significant creative mathematical genius produced since women began higher education.

Katherine Johnson worked at NASA in Virginia as one of its "computers", people who did complicated calculations by hand. As an African American woman in the segregated South, she faced unfair rules at work, at a time when the struggle for [[@equality|equal rights]] was still going on.

In 1962, before John Glenn became the first American to [[orbit|orbit]] the Earth, he asked that she check the electronic computer's numbers for his flight. She did, and he flew. Later she helped calculate paths for the [[@apollo-moon|Apollo Moon missions]]. In 2015 she received the Presidential Medal of Freedom.

Shakuntala Devi, born in Bengaluru in 1929, became famous as a "human computer". In 1980, at Imperial College London, she multiplied two 13-digit numbers in her head in 28 seconds, a feat recorded by Guinness [[@world-records|World Records]]. She toured the world showing that [[@mental-maths|mental maths]] could be fun.

Maryam Mirzakhani grew up in Tehran and became a professor at Stanford University. She studied the geometry of curved surfaces. In 2014 she became the first woman to win the Fields Medal, often called the highest prize in mathematics. She died in 2017, aged 40.

Today, many women continue the work. In India, the algebraist Raman Parimala has won major awards for her research. Girls in [[@maths-olympiad|maths olympiads]] around the world are adding new names to the list, much as [[@ramanujan|Ramanujan]] once did from a small town in Tamil Nadu.

text: Your voice comes from two small bands of muscle and tissue in your throat, called vocal folds. They sit inside the voice box, or [[larynx|larynx]]. When you speak, air from your lungs makes them vibrate hundreds of times a second, and that buzz becomes sound.

During puberty, [[@hormones|hormones]] tell the body to grow in many ways, and the larynx grows too. The vocal folds get longer and thicker. Longer, thicker folds vibrate more slowly, and slower [[vibration|vibrations]] make lower notes. So the voice gets deeper.
In boys, the larynx grows much more than in girls, so their voices drop by about an [[octave|octave]]. Girls' voices usually drop by just a few notes.

They get shorter and thinner
They stay the same and the mouth gets bigger

st.reveal: At puberty the voice box grows and the vocal folds become longer and thicker. Like a fat guitar string, they vibrate more slowly, so the voice sounds deeper. In boys they grow much more, so the change is bigger.

d.try: Stretch a rubber band between two fingers and pluck it. Now stretch it longer, or use a thicker band, and pluck again. Listen to how the note changes. Then put your fingers gently on your throat and hum a high note and a low note to feel your own vocal folds buzzing.
myth: Only boys' voices change during puberty.
Everyone's voice changes. Girls' voices usually drop by a few notes and become fuller, while boys' voices drop by about an octave, which is why their change is easier to hear.
facts: about 1.5–2.5 cm in men, a bit shorter in women

sec.t:
The change does not happen overnight. For several months, the folds are growing faster than the muscles that control them can adjust. It is like learning to play a guitar whose strings keep getting longer every week.

So a boy might start a sentence in a deep voice and suddenly squeak in the middle. That crack happens when control slips and the voice jumps to its old, higher setting. It is completely normal. For most people it settles down within a few months to a year. Girls go through a milder version too, and their voices can sound husky or wobbly for a while.

sec.h: The hidden bump in the neck

sec.t:
Scientists measure how fast vocal folds vibrate in hertz, which means buzzes per second. A young child's voice often sits around 250 to 300 hertz. An adult woman's speaking voice averages around 200 hertz, and an adult man's around 100 to 120.

So a man's vocal folds, when he talks, are flapping open and shut about 100 times every second. Hold a note for one minute and they will have opened and closed around 6,000 times.

Sound travels from your folds as waves of squeezed air. [[@sound-travel|Sound]] moves at about 343 metres per second through air, so a word you say reaches a friend across a classroom almost instantly.

For centuries, famous choirs relied on boys with high, clear voices. The trouble was that a boy's best singing years often ended just when he got good. In 1749, the teenage Joseph Haydn was let go from the choir of St Stephen's Cathedral in Vienna because his voice had broken. He went on to write more than 100 symphonies.

Today, many [[@choirs|choirs]] help singers through the change rather than sending them away. Voice teachers suggest singing gently in a comfortable range, drinking water and not shouting, while the voice settles. Some boys who sang high notes as children turn into strong tenors or deep basses later.

If a voice stays hoarse for weeks, or speaking hurts, it is a good idea to talk to a parent and a doctor. Usually, though, a cracking voice is just a sign that the body is right on schedule. And the same rule that sets your pitch explains why the fattest string on a [[@guitar|guitar]] makes the lowest, growliest note.

text: Boredom is the uncomfortable feeling of wanting to do something satisfying and not being able to. Your mind is restless and ready, but nothing around you holds its attention. Time seems to drag. You might fidget, sigh or keep checking the clock.

Scientists think boredom works like a signal. Hunger tells you that your body needs food. Boredom tells you that what you're doing isn't giving your brain enough to work with, or doesn't seem to matter. It nudges you to change something. That can lead to good things, like a new hobby, or bad ones, like doing something silly just to break the dullness.

sec.t:
In 2014, psychologists at the University of Virginia asked volunteers to sit [[@loneliness|alone]] in a plain room for about 15 minutes with nothing to do but think. Most found it unpleasant. Their minds wandered and they struggled to stay with their own thoughts.

In one version, the room had a button that gave a mild electric shock. Earlier, everyone had tried the shock and many said they would pay money to avoid feeling it again. Yet about two-thirds of the men and a quarter of the women pressed the button at least once while they were alone. One man pressed it 190 times. To many people, it seems, doing something unpleasant can feel better than doing nothing.

People have always felt dull and restless, but the word "boredom" is young. English speakers used "bore" to describe a dull person or thing in the 1700s. "Boredom" only became common in the 1850s. [[@charles-dickens|Charles Dickens]] used it in his novel *Bleak House*, about a rich lady who is bored to death, and that helped spread it.

Other languages had their own words much earlier, such as the French *ennui*. Hindi speakers might say *bore ho raha hoon*, borrowing the English word.

Some studies suggest that a dull spell can lead to more creative thinking. In one British experiment, people who first spent time copying numbers from a phone book later came up with more ideas for uses of plastic cups than people who hadn't. The idea is that a bored mind starts to wander and make new connections. Scientists are still testing how strong this effect really is.

Boredom may also push people towards goals. Feeling stuck can be the spark that sends someone off to learn guitar, start a garden or write a story.

Today, many people never have to sit with boredom. A phone fills every queue, car journey and quiet moment. That isn't always bad, but some researchers worry that we lose the chance to daydream, plan or simply notice the world. Thinking about your [[@screen-time|screen time]] is one way to give your mind a little empty space.

If boredom turns into a long-lasting feeling that nothing is worth doing, that can be a sign of low mood. It's worth talking to a parent, teacher or doctor about it. Most boredom, though, is just your brain asking for a better challenge.

text: Braces straighten teeth by pushing on them gently, all day and all night, for months or years. Small metal or ceramic pieces called brackets are glued to the front of each tooth. A springy wire runs through all the brackets and is bent into the shape of a perfect smile.
The wire keeps trying to spring back into that shape. As it does, it pulls and pushes each tooth a tiny bit.

A tooth isn't fixed in solid rock. It sits in a socket of living bone, held by a thin cushion of fibres. Steady pressure makes the bone slowly rebuild itself around the tooth, letting it travel to a new place.

A very hard push for a few minutes a day
Pulling on the teeth only while you sleep

st.reveal: Light, steady pressure gives the bone cells time to clear a path in front of the tooth and build new bone behind it. Pushing too hard squashes the blood vessels in the gum and can actually slow the movement down.

myth: Braces are only for children and teenagers.

Bone is rebuilt at every age, so adults can have braces too. Treatment can take a little longer because adult bone changes more slowly, but many people get braces in their twenties, thirties or later.

sec.h: Bone that moves out of the way
sec.t:
Your [[@bones|bones]] look hard and still, but they are busy. Special cells keep tearing down old bone and laying down new bone, all your life.

When a brace pushes a tooth, the fibres on one side get squashed and the fibres on the other side get stretched. On the squashed side, cells called osteoclasts start [[dissolve|dissolving]] bone, opening up room for the tooth to move into. On the stretched side, cells called osteoblasts build fresh bone to fill the gap left behind.

A tooth usually moves about a millimetre a month. That sounds slow, but over two years it can add up to more than the width of a whole tooth.

Why do teeth grow crooked at all? Sometimes the jaw is a little too small for the teeth, so they crowd and twist. Sometimes the top and bottom jaws grow at different rates, and habits like long-term thumb-sucking can push front teeth forward. Often it simply runs in families.

Many braces today use wires made of nickel and titanium. This metal can be bent at room temperature and then, warmed in the mouth, it tries to return to its first shape. So it keeps up a gentle pull for weeks.

Every month or two, a dentist who specialises in straightening teeth, called an [[orthodontist|orthodontist]], changes or adjusts the wire. Teeth often ache for a day or two afterwards, which is a sign the bone cells have work to do.

Tiny rubber bands hooked between the top and bottom teeth help line up the bite, the way the jaws close together. Wearers often pick a new colour of band at each visit.

{{story:springs}}

People have tried to straighten teeth for a very long time. In 1728 a French dentist, Pierre Fauchard, described a curved strip of metal tied to the teeth to widen the arch. In the late 1800s and early 1900s an American dentist named Edward Angle sorted bites into types and designed many brace parts, and he is often called the father of modern orthodontics.

Clear plastic aligners arrived in the USA in 1998. Instead of a wire, you wear a series of thin trays, each shaped a fraction differently from the last. Computers plan the steps, and many trays are made using [[@3d-printing|3D printers]].

When braces come off, the job isn't over. The fibres around each tooth remember where it used to be and slowly tug it back. So most people wear a retainer, a plastic tray or a thin wire glued behind the teeth, for years afterwards.

Braces also make cleaning harder. Food gets stuck around the brackets, and if it isn't brushed away it can lead to [[@tooth-decay|tooth decay]] and white marks on the teeth. Orthodontists often give wearers small brushes to clean between the wires. And no, braces won't set off an airport metal detector or pick up radio stations.

text: A habit is something you do automatically when you're in a [[@mystery-deja-vu|familiar situation]]. You walk in the door and drop your bag in the same spot. You sit at the table and reach for the same chair. You didn't decide. Your brain just did it.

Habits form through repetition. Each time you do something in the same place or at the same time, and it ends well, the link between the situation and the action gets stronger. After enough repeats, the situation alone triggers the action. Habits live in a different kind of [[@memory|memory]] from facts, the kind that also holds skills like riding a bicycle.
That's why habits are hard to break. The trigger is still there, and the brain still reaches for the old routine, whether or not you want it to.

st.prompt: Volunteers in a London study tried to make a new daily habit, like eating fruit at lunch. How long did it take on average before it felt automatic?

66 days

st.reveal: The average was 66 days, but people varied hugely, from 18 days to more than 250. Simple habits, like drinking water, came faster than harder ones, like doing exercises. Missing a single day didn't spoil the process.

myth: It takes exactly 21 days to form a new habit.

The 21-day idea comes from a 1960 self-help book by a surgeon, Maxwell Maltz, who said people took a minimum of about 21 days to adjust to changes. When scientists measured habit-building, it took about 66 days on average, with huge differences between people.

sec.t:
Scientists often describe a habit as a loop with three parts. First there's a cue, the trigger: a time, a place, a feeling or a sound. Then the routine, the thing you do. Last comes the reward, a good feeling that tells your brain the routine was worth remembering.

The brain chemical [[dopamine|dopamine]] helps with this learning. When a routine pays off, dopamine helps strengthen the connection. Over time the brain starts expecting the reward as soon as it spots the cue. A phone buzz is a cue. Checking it is the routine. A new message is the reward. Designers of [[@social-media|social media]] apps understand this loop very well.

In 2009, researchers at University College London asked 96 volunteers to pick a new daily habit and track it for 12 weeks. Some chose to drink a glass of water at breakfast. Others chose to run before dinner.

On average, it took 66 days for the action to feel automatic. But one person got there in 18 days, and for some it would have taken longer than eight months. Easy habits formed faster. Missing the odd day didn't ruin anything, which is good news for anyone who slips up.

Willpower alone is a weak tool against a habit, because the habit runs faster than your decisions. Researchers suggest changing the situation instead. If the cue never appears, the routine doesn't start. Leaving a phone in another room at bedtime works better than promising yourself not to check it.

Another trick is to keep the cue but swap the routine. If you snack when you're [[@boredom|bored]] after school, keep a fruit bowl where the biscuit tin used to be. The brain still gets a reward, just a different one, and the new loop slowly takes over the old one.

text: Artificial intelligence, or AI, means computer systems that do tasks that normally need human intelligence: recognising faces, understanding speech, translating languages, playing games, answering questions and more.

Most AI today works through machine learning. Instead of following rules written by a programmer for every situation, the system is shown huge numbers of examples and finds patterns in them. Shown millions of photos, it learns to spot cats. Trained on vast amounts of text, it learns to write sentences that sound human.
AI is powerful, but it isn't magic, and it doesn't think the way people do. Whether it understands anything at all is still hotly debated.

st.reveal: Writing rules for every possible cat is almost impossible. They learn from examples, though they usually need far more of them than a child does.

sec.t:
In 1950, the British mathematician [[@alan-turing|Alan Turing]] asked whether machines could think. Since "thinking" is hard to define, he suggested a test. If a person chatting by text couldn't tell whether they were talking to a human or a machine, the machine could be said to behave intelligently. This became known as the Turing test.

In 1955, the American computer scientist John McCarthy and colleagues proposed a summer workshop at Dartmouth College to explore "artificial intelligence". It took place in 1956, and the name stuck.

Early AI used hand-written rules. Programs could solve [[@puzzles-logic|logic puzzles]] and play draughts. But real life has too many exceptions for rules alone. How do you write rules for every way a person can write the letter "a"?

Machine learning took a different path. One popular kind uses artificial [[@neural-networks|neural networks]], loosely inspired by how nerve cells in [[@brain-works|the brain]] connect. The network starts out making random guesses. Each time it gets something wrong, it adjusts millions of tiny settings. After enough examples, it gets very good. This needs powerful computers and lots of data, which is why AI took off in the 2010s.

Recent [[@chatbots|chatbots]] are built on [[@large-language-models|large language models]]. They are trained on vast amounts of text to predict which word is likely to come next. Doing this well, at huge scale, lets them answer questions, write stories and help with homework.

But they can make things up, a problem often called "hallucination". They can repeat unfair ideas found in their training data. They have no real experience of the world. So it's wise to check important facts, and [[@future-schools|many schools]] have rules about using AI for work.

AI helps doctors [[@future-medicine|spot signs of disease in scans]] and helps scientists improve [[@weather-forecasts|weather forecasts]]. An AI system called AlphaFold predicts the 3D shapes of [[protein|proteins]], the tiny machines inside living cells. Its creators shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

In India, the government's Bhashini project uses AI to help people [[@translation|translate]] between Indian languages and speak to apps in their own language. [[@self-driving|Self-driving cars]], [[@voice-assistants|voice assistants]] and recommendations on streaming apps all use AI.

People disagree about where this is heading. Some expect AI to help cure diseases and solve hard problems. Others worry about [[@future-jobs-ai|jobs]], [[@ai-safety|fairness]], false information and machines that are hard to control. Many governments are now writing rules for how AI can be used. What's certain is that underneath, it still runs on ordinary [[@computers-how|computer chips]], following [[@algorithms|algorithms]] that people designed.

text: Future clothes may be able to sense, cool, heat, heal and even talk to your phone. Scientists are building fabrics with [[sensor|sensors]] woven in to measure heartbeat and breathing. Others are working on cloth that keeps you cool on a hot day without any electricity, coats that warm up on cold mornings, and fibres that clean themselves.

Some of these already exist. You can buy shirts that track your heart rate and running socks that measure your steps. Others are still in labs. The big challenges are making them comfortable, washable and cheap, and finding a way to recycle them when they wear out. Electronics hate water, and clothes go through the wash dozens of times a year.

st.prompt: How can a fabric keep you cooler than cotton, without any power?

options.t: It lets your body's infrared heat pass straight through, instead of trapping it
It contains tiny fans woven into the threads
It holds ice crystals inside its fibres

st.reveal: Your body gives off heat partly as infrared light, which you can't see. Cotton absorbs much of it. Some new fabrics are clear to infrared but still block visible light, so they look normal while letting heat escape.

sec.t:
In 2017, Google and Levi's sold a denim jacket with a touch-sensitive patch on its sleeve. Swipe it, and your phone skipped a song or read out directions. The threads in the patch were made of fine metal wrapped around cotton.

Doctors are interested in shirts that measure heartbeat, breathing and temperature all day. They could help people with heart problems, or alert parents if a baby has trouble breathing. Today, a [[@smartwatches|smartwatch]] does some of this on your wrist. A shirt touches far more of your skin, so it might measure more accurately.

Many clothing ideas come from space. NASA developed materials that store and release heat, called phase-change materials, to keep astronauts comfortable. Some of these now appear in jackets, gloves and mattresses. Memory foam and some sportswear fibres also have roots in space research.

[[@spiders-silk|Spider silk]] is famous for being strong and stretchy. Spiders are hard to farm, because they eat each other. So companies are using [[yeast|yeast]] and [[bacteria|bacteria]] to brew silk proteins in tanks, then spinning them into thread. A few products, including a jacket and a tie, have been made this way in small numbers.

Some fabrics change colour with heat or light, like a mood ring. Others use tiny electronics to switch patterns. Scientists study animals such as the [[@power-chameleon|chameleon]] and the cuttlefish, which change colour using special skin cells.

Military researchers have tried fabrics that blend into their surroundings. Fashion designers have made dresses that glow with LEDs or shift colour as you move. At a 2016 gala in New York, one actress wore a gown woven with optical fibres that glowed when the lights went down. For now, most of these are one-off designs, not everyday wear.

Clothes already create huge amounts of waste. Every year, millions of tonnes of old clothes are thrown away. Smart clothes, with wires and chips, could make this worse, adding to the growing pile of [[@e-waste|e-waste]].

So some researchers are working on clothes that can be taken apart, or made from materials that break down safely. India has an old answer too. [[@khadi|Khadi]], hand-spun and hand-woven cotton, is simple, breathable and long-lasting. The future of clothes may mix space-age fibres with very old ideas: wear things longer, repair them and choose fabrics that suit the [[climate|climate]].

text: India built its first satellites [[@india-space-budget|with very little money]], borrowed equipment and a lot of determination. The space programme began in the 1960s under the scientist [[@vikram-sarabhai|Vikram Sarabhai]], who believed space technology could help a poor country with [[@weather-forecasts|weather forecasts]], education and communication.

Indian engineers first learned with small [[@rockets-how|sounding rockets]], which shoot up and fall back down. Then they designed a satellite, [[@space-aryabhata-satellite|Aryabhata]], in a group of sheds in Peenya, an industrial area of [[@bengaluru|Bengaluru]]. It was launched on a Soviet rocket on 19 April 1975. Five years later, in 1980, India launched a satellite on a rocket of its own.

st.prompt: India's first satellite, Aryabhata, was launched in 1975. Whose rocket carried it into space?

options.t: A rocket from the Soviet Union
An Indian rocket from Sriharikota

st.reveal: India built the satellite, but it didn't yet have a rocket big enough to reach orbit. The Soviet Union launched Aryabhata free of charge from a site in Russia. India's own rocket, SLV-3, put a satellite in orbit five years later.

myth: India launched its first satellite on its own rocket.
Aryabhata, India's first satellite, was built in India but launched by the Soviet Union in 1975. India's first satellite launch on its own rocket came in 1980, when SLV-3 carried Rohini into orbit.
facts: First satellite on an Indian rocket

sec.t:
In the early 1960s, scientists chose Thumba, a fishing village near Thiruvananthapuram in [[@kerala|Kerala]], as India's first rocket launch site. Thumba lies close to the magnetic [[equator|equator]], which made it a good place to study the upper [[atmosphere|atmosphere]].

The local church, St Mary Magdalene, was handed over to the scientists. It became an office and workshop, and the bishop's house became a laboratory. On 21 November 1963, a small American-made rocket called a Nike-Apache rose from Thumba. A famous photograph shows [[@space-rocket-bicycle|rocket parts being carried on a bicycle]]. The church is now a space museum.

In 1969, the Indian Space Research Organisation, ISRO, was formed. Soon after, its engineers started work on a satellite. Most had never built one. They had to make or adapt almost everything themselves, from solar panels to radio equipment.

Aryabhata, named after the great Indian mathematician [[@aryabhata|Aryabhata]], was a 26-sided shape about 1.4 metres across, covered in solar cells. It weighed about 360 kg. The Soviet Union offered to launch it, and on 19 April 1975 it lifted off from a site in Russia.

After a few days in [[orbit|orbit]], a power problem stopped its experiments. But the satellite had proved India could design, build and control a spacecraft. The Reserve Bank of India later printed Aryabhata on the back of the two-rupee note.

{{story:isro-missions}}

India also needed its own rocket to reach orbit. The SLV-3 project was led by a young engineer named A.P.J. Abdul Kalam, who later became President of India. Its first attempt, in 1979, failed and fell into the sea. Kalam later wrote that ISRO's chairman, Satish Dhawan, faced the press himself and took the blame. When the next launch succeeded, Dhawan let Kalam announce the good news.

On 18 July 1980, SLV-3 lifted off from Sriharikota, an island off the coast of Andhra Pradesh, and placed the small Rohini satellite in orbit. India had joined the small group of countries that could launch satellites on their own rockets.

sec.h: A satellite on a bullock cart
sec.t:
In 1981 came APPLE, India's first experimental communications satellite. It was launched by a European rocket. Before launch, engineers needed to test its antenna away from metal objects that might interfere. So they put it on a wooden bullock cart. A photograph of the shiny satellite riding the cart became one of the best-known pictures in Indian science.

Those small beginnings led to [[@satellite-tv|INSAT satellites]] for TV and weather in the 1980s, and to the PSLV rocket, which in 2017 launched 104 satellites on a single flight. The country that once carried rockets on [[@bicycles-history|bicycles]] later reached the Moon and Mars.

text: For most of history, nobody knew what germs were. Doctors guessed at why people got sick and tried whatever seemed to help. Some cures were useless, some were harmful, and a few accidentally worked.

People ate powdered mummies, drained blood out of the sick, swallowed potions with 60 ingredients and blew smoke into very unusual places. Strange as these sound, a few old remedies led straight to medicines still in your cupboard. Please don't try any of them. Even the ones that partly worked were risky, and a doctor today has far better tools.

st.prompt: In the 1700s, London had a kit for reviving people pulled out of rivers. What did it use?

options.t: A tube to blow tobacco smoke into the patient's bottom
A bucket of ice to wake them with cold
A trumpet to blast in their ear

st.reveal: People believed tobacco smoke would warm the body and restart breathing. Kits were kept near the River Thames. It did not work, and doctors gave it up in the early 1800s once they learned more about the heart and lungs.

d.try: Make a "medicine detective" chart. List five old cures from this article in one column. In the next, write whether you think it worked, failed, or partly worked, and why. Then ask a trusted adult or look it up together to check your guesses.
myth: People in the past were foolish to believe in such strange cures.
They were working with the best ideas they had, before anyone knew about germs or could test medicines fairly. Some old cures, like willow bark and honey, turned out to contain real medicine.
facts: Blood taken from George Washington in 1799
Leeches approved as a medical device in the USA
1899, based on a chemical found in willow bark
Ingredients in some old theriac recipes

sec.t:
In the 1500s, European chemists stocked a brown powder called *mumia*. It was made by grinding up bodies taken from Egyptian tombs. People swallowed it for bruises, headaches and almost anything else.

The idea started with a mix-up. An Arabic word, *mumiya*, meant a natural black tar that was used as a medicine. Ancient Egyptian [[@mummies|mummies]] looked as if they were coated in the same dark stuff, so traders began selling the mummies themselves. Demand grew so high that some sellers made fakes from the bodies of recently dead people. The fashion faded in the 1700s.

For over 2,000 years, many doctors believed the body held four fluids, and illness meant one was out of balance. The cure was to let some [[@blood|blood]] out, by cutting a [[vein|vein]] or by putting hungry leeches on the skin.

When George Washington, the first US president, fell ill with a throat [[infection|infection]] in 1799, his doctors took about 2.4 litres of his blood in less than a day. That is around 40 percent of what an adult body holds. He died that night. Most historians think the bleeding made things worse.

Leeches have made a comeback, though. [[surgeon|Surgeons]] use them after reattaching fingers or ears, because their spit stops blood clotting and keeps it flowing through fragile new veins.

{{story:sushruta}}

One of the most famous medicines in Europe and the Middle East was *theriac*. Some recipes had more than 60 ingredients, including opium, honey, spices and dried snake meat. Cities like Venice made it in public, so buyers could watch and be sure it wasn't fake. Theriac was meant to cure almost anything, from snakebite to plague. Some doctors in Europe still prescribed it in the 1800s.

In the 1920s, some Americans paid for "radium water", which contained a [[radioactive|radioactive]] metal. People thought the glow meant energy. It actually caused terrible illness, and it helped scientists understand how dangerous [[radiation|radiation]] is.

Not every old cure was a dud. For thousands of years, people in Egypt, Greece and India chewed willow bark for pain and fever. In the 1800s, chemists found the active chemical inside. In 1899, the company Bayer turned a version of it into aspirin.

Ancient Egyptian doctors smeared [[@honey|honey]] on wounds. Honey makes it hard for [[bacteria|bacteria]] to grow, and some hospitals still use specially cleaned medical honey on hard-to-heal cuts. In ancient India, the surgeon Sushruta described using leeches and careful stitching, and his writings show a sharp eye for how wounds heal.

sec.h: Why bad cures seemed to work
sec.t:
Many patients felt better after weird treatments. Partly that is because most illnesses get better on their own. Partly it is the [[@placebo|placebo]] effect, where believing in a cure can make you feel better even if it does nothing. Without fair tests, nobody could tell the difference.

Fair tests, where one group gets the medicine and another doesn't, only became normal in the 1900s. Around the same time, a scientist noticed mould killing bacteria on a dish, and the age of [[@antibiotics|antibiotics]] began.

text: Bangladesh is a country to India's east, almost wrapped around by West Bengal, Assam, [[@meghalaya|Meghalaya]], Tripura and Mizoram, with the Bay of Bengal to the south. It is one of the most crowded countries on Earth. About 17 crore people live in an area a little smaller than Odisha.

Almost the whole country is a giant [[delta|delta]], the low, flat land built up where [[@rivers-himalaya|the Ganga]], the [[@brahmaputra|Brahmaputra]] and the Meghna rivers reach the sea. It is green, wet and full of rivers. People here speak [[@bengali-language|Bangla]], the same language spoken in West Bengal, and share much of the food, music and poetry of Bengal.

d.try: Fill a long baking tray with sand or soil, raise one end slightly, and slowly pour water at the top. Watch how the water spreads out into many small channels and drops sand where it slows down at the bottom. That fan of mud is a tiny delta.
myth: Floods are always a disaster for Bangladesh.

Ordinary monsoon floods are part of farming life. They spread fresh silt over the fields and make the soil rich. It is the rare, extreme floods that destroy homes and crops, and Bangladeshis use different words for the two kinds.

sec.t:
In 1947, British India was divided, as told in [[@partition|Partition]]. The area that is now Bangladesh became East Pakistan, part of Pakistan, though it lay more than 1,500 km from West Pakistan, with India in between.

In 1948 the government announced that Urdu alone would be the national language. Most people in East Pakistan spoke Bangla, and many felt their language and culture were being pushed aside. On 21 February 1952, police opened fire on student protesters in Dhaka, killing several. That day is remembered with flowers and songs at the Shaheed Minar in Dhaka.

Tensions grew over the next twenty years. In 1971, after a brutal crackdown by the Pakistani army, a war of independence broke out. Millions of [[refugee|refugees]] fled to India. India joined the war in December, and on 16 December 1971 the Pakistani forces in the east surrendered. Bangladesh, meaning "land of the Bengalis", became independent.

The national anthem, "Amar Shonar Bangla" ("My Golden Bengal"), is a song by [[@tagore|Rabindranath Tagore]]. He wrote it in 1905, long before Bangladesh existed. He also wrote "Jana Gana Mana", so one poet gave words to two neighbouring countries.

Dhaka is one of the most crowded cities in the world, and its streets are famous for cycle rickshaws painted with bright pictures of film stars, birds and flowers. Jute, a tough plant fibre used for sacks and ropes, was once Bangladesh's main [[export|export]] and was nicknamed the "golden fibre".

Today the biggest industry is clothing. Bangladesh is one of the world's largest exporters of ready-made clothes, after China. There is a fair chance that a T-shirt in your cupboard was stitched there, a story you can follow in [[@clothes-cotton|cotton and clothes]].

[[@cyclones-india|Cyclones from the Bay of Bengal]] sometimes strike the coast. In 1970, a terrible [[cyclone|cyclone]] killed hundreds of thousands of people. Since then, Bangladesh has built thousands of cyclone shelters on stilts and set up warning systems run partly by volunteers with megaphones.

Death tolls from big storms have dropped hugely as a result. Bangladesh has become a place that other countries study to learn how to live with rising water.

text: The Golden Gate Bridge is a suspension bridge. Two tall towers stand in the water, and two thick cables loop over them from shore to shore. Hundreds of thinner ropes hang down from those cables and hold up the road.

Workers built it between 1933 and 1937 across the Golden Gate, the windy strait where San Francisco Bay meets the Pacific Ocean. They had to fight fierce currents, thick fog and strong winds. When it opened, its main span of 1,280 metres was the longest of any suspension bridge on Earth.

st.reveal: The steel arrived coated in reddish primer, and the consulting architect Irving Morrow liked it. He chose a shade now called International Orange because it blends with the landscape yet stays visible in fog.

The bridge isn't repainted end to end on a loop. A team of painters works all year, touching up spots where salty fog has damaged the paint and steel.

sec.t:
For years, people said the Golden Gate could not be bridged. The water is more than 100 metres deep in places, tides rush through it, and fog rolls in almost every summer afternoon. Ferries carried people across instead.

The engineer Joseph Strauss pushed for a bridge for over a decade. Much of the hard maths was done by another engineer, Charles Ellis, whose part was forgotten for years. Work began in January 1933, during the [[@great-depression|Great Depression]], and the jobs mattered to thousands of families.

The main cables were not lifted into place in one piece. Machines carried single wires back and forth over the towers, again and again, like a spider spinning a web. Each cable holds 27,572 wires, packed into a bundle almost a metre thick.

Altogether there is enough wire in the two cables to circle the Earth about three times. Once the cables were done, workers hung the road deck from them, section by section, working out from the towers so the weight stayed balanced.

A suspension bridge is meant to bend a little. In strong winds the road can swing several metres sideways, and on hot days the steel stretches so the middle of the deck sags lower. The engineers planned for all of this. A bridge that could not move would be more likely to crack.

Bridge building in the 1930s was dangerous. Strauss insisted that workers wear hard hats, which was unusual then, and he paid for a huge net to be strung under the bridge. It caught 19 men who fell. They joked that they had joined the Halfway to Hell Club.

Even so, 11 workers died, ten of them in a single accident in February 1937 when a platform tore through the net. Their names are remembered at the bridge. The safety rules Strauss pushed for, from hard hats to nets, helped change how big building sites were run across the country.

The bridge opened to walkers on 27 May 1937, and about 200,000 people crossed on foot that day. Cars came the next day. It held the world record for the longest suspension span until 1964, when the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge in New York beat it.

It is now one of the most photographed places in [[@san-francisco|San Francisco]], often with its towers poking out of the fog. Kolkata's [[@howrah-bridge|Howrah Bridge]], finished a few years later in 1943, is a different design that needs no cables at all. It holds its road up with steel arms that reach out from each bank.

text: The Shore Temple is a stone temple standing right on the beach at Mahabalipuram, about 55 km south of [[@chennai|Chennai]]. It was built in the early 700s CE by the Pallava king Narasimhavarman II, also known as Rajasimha. It has two shrines to Shiva and one to Vishnu, and its towers rise in neat stepped layers like a pyramid.

It is one of the oldest structural stone temples in South India. Instead of carving a temple out of a single rock, its builders stacked cut [[granite|granite]] blocks. Sea winds and salt have worn the carvings soft, but the temple still stands, more than 1,300 years later.

st.reveal: Sailors saw the temple towers from out at sea and used them to find their way along the coast. They called the site the Seven Pagodas, which led to legends that six more temples lay under the waves.

myth: The Shore Temple was carved out of a single rock, like Mahabalipuram's other monuments.

Many famous monuments at Mahabalipuram are cut from one rock. The Shore Temple is different. It was built from cut granite blocks stacked together, making it one of the earliest important stone temples built this way in South India.

sec.t:
In the 600s and 700s, the [[@pallavas|Pallavas]] ruled much of South India from their capital at Kanchipuram. Mahabalipuram, then called Mamallapuram, was their busy port. Ships sailed from here to Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia, carrying goods, ideas and even architects.

The town is named after King Narasimhavarman I, nicknamed Mamalla, "the great wrestler". Under him and his successors, sculptors turned the area's granite hills into a giant open-air workshop. Stone carving never left the town. Today hundreds of sculptors still work in Mahabalipuram's streets, and the tapping of chisels on granite can be heard from morning till evening. Their gods and elephants are shipped to temples across India and abroad.

Earlier monuments at Mahabalipuram were carved straight out of boulders and cliffs. There are cave temples, the five Rathas cut from single rocks, and a huge carved rock face called Arjuna's Penance, or the Descent of the Ganga.

The Shore Temple was a step forward. Builders cut granite blocks, shaped them and stacked them into towers, with carvings added on top. That method later made giant temples possible, like the Chola temple at [[@india-wonder-brihadeeswara|Thanjavur]], built about 300 years later.

European sailors once called Mahabalipuram the Seven Pagodas. The name led to a legend that seven temples once stood here, and the sea swallowed six. For centuries, people wondered if there was any truth in it.

On 26 December 2004, the Indian Ocean [[@tsunami|tsunami]] struck. Just before the wave hit, the sea pulled back hundreds of metres. People saw rows of stones and carvings that had been underwater for ages. Afterwards, sand washed away from the beach revealed a large stone lion and other carvings. Divers have since found remains of walls and structures offshore, though how old they are is still being studied.

The sea has always been the temple's biggest danger. Waves and salt eat away at the stone. In the 1990s and 2000s, the Archaeological Survey of India built a stone wall, called a groyne, and planted trees to protect it. Experts also treat the stone to stop salt damage.

In 1984, UNESCO named the Shore Temple and the other Mahabalipuram monuments a World Heritage Site. Each winter, the Mamallapuram Dance Festival brings classical dancers to perform near Arjuna's Penance, with the sea breeze blowing.

The sea gives, and the sea takes. Along coasts around the world, waves slowly [[@cliffs-erosion|carve away cliffs]], and the Shore Temple's builders seem to have known that only the hardest granite could last.

text: For thousands of years, the lands that are now India and Pakistan had one long, shared history. In 1947, when British rule ended, the [[subcontinent|subcontinent]] was divided into two countries. India and Pakistan have been neighbours ever since, and their governments have often disagreed, sometimes fought.

But people on both sides still share a great deal. They share the oldest cities of the region, the Indus River, the history of the Mughals and much more. They speak closely related languages and cook many of the same dishes. They watch the same films and songs, and both are passionate about cricket.

sec.t:
In August 1947, British India was split into India and Pakistan. Pakistan then included two parts, West and East, with East Pakistan later becoming [[@bangladesh|Bangladesh]]. The new border cut through Punjab and Bengal, through farms, villages and families.

Around 1.5 crore people crossed the new borders, Hindus and Sikhs moving to India and Muslims moving to Pakistan. It was one of the largest migrations in history. There was terrible violence, and estimates of the dead range from a few hundred thousand to about two million. Many families on both sides still have grandparents who remember leaving a home they never saw again.

If a person from Delhi and a person from Lahore chat about cricket or food, they will understand each other easily. Everyday Hindi and [[@urdu|Urdu]] are so close that some people call the shared spoken language Hindustani. [[@film-songs|Film songs]] from Mumbai are loved in Pakistan for exactly that reason.

The difference shows on paper. Hindi is written in Devanagari, from left to right. [[@arabic-script|Urdu]] is written in a flowing Perso-Arabic script, from right to left. In formal speech, Hindi often borrows words from Sanskrit, and Urdu from Persian and Arabic. [[@punjabi-gurmukhi|Punjabi]], too, is spoken on both sides, written in Gurmukhi in India and in Shahmukhi in Pakistan.

Kebabs, biryani, parathas, lassi and sweet milky [[@food-chai-history|chai]] are loved in both countries. Each side argues happily about whose [[@biryani|biryani]] is best.

The Mughal emperors ruled from both Delhi and Lahore, as told in [[@mughals|the Mughals]]. Lahore Fort and the Badshahi Mosque in Pakistan, and the Red Fort and Jama Masjid in India, were built by the same [[dynasty|dynasty]]. Ancient Taxila, near Islamabad, was a famous centre of learning linked by tradition with [[@chanakya|Chanakya]], the adviser of Chandragupta Maurya.

When India and Pakistan play [[@cricket-history|cricket]], streets on both sides fall quiet. These matches are among the most watched sporting events on Earth.

At the Attari-Wagah crossing between Amritsar and Lahore, soldiers from both countries have held a flag-lowering ceremony at sunset for decades. It is full of high kicks, stamping and loud cheers from crowds on each side.

Many families still have relatives across the border, and some write, call and visit when they can.

text: India has an enormous treasure of folk tales, told in hundreds of languages. Some of the best known are the animal fables of the [[@panchatantra-tales|Panchatantra]] and the Jataka tales of the Buddha's past lives. Others are the ghost story-riddles of [[@vikram-betal|Vikram and Betal]], and the funny tales of clever courtiers like Birbal and [[@tenali-raman|Tenali Raman]].

Most of these stories were passed on by voice long before anyone wrote them down. Grandparents told them at bedtime, travelling storytellers performed them at fairs, and puppeteers and singers acted them out. Each teller changed them a little, so the same story can have dozens of versions.

st.prompt: In the old story of the monkey and the crocodile, how does the monkey escape when he learns the crocodile wants to eat his heart?

options.t: He says he left his heart in the tree, and asks to go back for it
He jumps over the river in one huge leap
He calls an elephant to help

st.reveal: Riding on the crocodile's back in the middle of the river, the monkey claims he keeps his heart up in his tree. The crocodile swims back to fetch it, and the monkey leaps to safety. The story appears in both the Panchatantra and the Jataka tales.

src: Ramanujan A. K. (1991) Folktales from India. Pantheon Books.
Encyclopaedia Britannica, Panchatantra; Kathasaritsagara.
Mitra Majumdar D. (1907) Thakurmar Jhuli.
n.certNote: Folk tales were passed on by word of mouth, so nobody knows exactly when most of them began. Dates for old collections like the Panchatantra are estimates, and scholars give ranges of several hundred years.
