d.try: Ask the oldest person in your family to tell you a story they heard as a child. Listen without writing, then retell it the next day to someone else. Compare your version with theirs. You'll notice you changed small things without meaning to, which is exactly how folk tales grow and shift.
myth: Folk tales are just simple stories for small children.

Many Indian folk tales were made for adults too. They carry lessons about power, politics, friendship and trickery, and some, like the riddles of Vikram and Betal, are puzzles that have kept grown-ups arguing for centuries.
facts: A. K. Ramanujan's 1991 collection from 22 languages

sec.t:
The Panchatantra, meaning "five books", is a set of animal fables said to have been written by a wise teacher, Vishnu Sharma, to teach three lazy princes how to rule. Lions, jackals, crows, tortoises and monkeys argue, plot and make friends. A tortoise who can't keep his mouth shut falls from the sky. A clever rabbit tricks a lion into jumping into a well at his own reflection.

The stories are nested like boxes. One character starts telling a tale, and inside it another character tells another, so a single book holds dozens of stories within stories.

The Jataka tales tell similar stories, with the future Buddha as a wise animal or person. The monkey and crocodile story appears in both collections.

Many favourite Indian tales star a clever courtier who outwits proud nobles and teaches the king a lesson. [[@akbar-birbal|Akbar and Birbal]] are set at the Mughal court. Birbal was a real minister, though most of the stories were made up much later.

In the south, Tenali Raman is linked to King Krishnadevaraya of [[@vijayanagara|Vijayanagara]] in the 1500s. In Bengal, Gopal Bhar plays tricks at the court of a Nadia king. Sheikh Chilli, a lovable daydreamer whose plans always collapse, is known across north India and Pakistan.

Every region has its own stories. In Bengal, *Thakurmar Jhuli*, "Grandmother's Bag", printed in 1907, collected tales of princes, demons and talking birds, and children still read it. In Rajasthan, the writer Vijaydan Detha spent decades collecting folk tales from villagers. One became the Hindi film *Paheli*.

The 11th-century Kashmiri writer Somadeva put together the *Kathasaritsagara*, "Ocean of the Streams of Story", one of the largest story collections ever made. It includes the Vikram and Betal tales. In each, a ghost tells the king a story ending in a riddle. If the king knows the answer and stays silent, his head will burst into pieces.

In 1991, the poet and scholar A. K. Ramanujan published *Folktales from India*, with stories gathered from 22 languages. Since 1967, the comic series [[@amar-chitra-katha|Amar Chitra Katha]] has retold folk tales for millions of children, and cartoons and films keep borrowing them. Like all folk tales, they keep changing, and that is how they survive. A story told in a Tamil village today may differ from a Punjabi version in its heroes, its jokes and its ending, and both count as the real thing.

text: The Jataka tales are stories of the earlier lives of the [[@buddha|Buddha]]. Buddhists believe that before he was born as Prince Siddhartha, he lived many lives. Sometimes he was a human, and often an animal: a monkey, a deer, an elephant, a quail, a hare. In each life he practised a virtue, such as generosity, patience or courage, preparing for the life in which he would become enlightened.

The main collection, in the Pali language, has about 550 stories. Many are short, funny or moving [[fable|fables]]. Some are long adventures with kings, merchants and [[@myths-indian-creatures|magical beings]].

st.prompt: In the Sasa Jataka, what does the god Sakka draw on the Moon?

options.t: A hare
A monkey
A lotus flower

st.reveal: The hare offers itself as food to a hungry stranger, who turns out to be the god Sakka in disguise. Moved by its generosity, Sakka draws the hare on the Moon so that everyone will remember.

src: Cowell E.B. (ed., 1895–1907) The Jātaka, or Stories of the Buddha's Former Births. Cambridge University Press.
UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Buddhist Monuments at Sanchi.
Encyclopaedia Britannica, Jataka.
n.certNote: The Jataka collection is well documented, and some of its stories were carved in stone over 2,000 years ago. Buddhists understand the tales as the Buddha's past lives. Historians study them as an ancient collection, many of whose stories are older than Buddhism.

d.try: On the next clear night near full Moon, look at the Moon with a family member from a window, balcony or garden. Try to find the shape of a hare in the dark patches. Draw what you see, then look up how people in other countries describe the shapes, such as a face, a rabbit or a woman reading.
myth: The Jataka tales were all invented by Buddhists.
Many of the stories were folk tales already told across India. Buddhist storytellers adapted them, giving the hero's role to the Buddha-to-be. Some of the same stories turn up in the Panchatantra.
facts: stories of the Buddha's past lives
Bharhut and Sanchi, over 2,000 years ago

sec.t:
Most Jataka tales follow a pattern. They begin in the present, with the Buddha hearing about something that happened among his followers. He then tells a story from long ago, which usually opens "Once upon a time, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares". At the end, he explains which of today's people played which part in the past.

The Buddha-to-be is called the Bodhisatta, the Pali form of Bodhisattva, "a being on the way to awakening". Many of the tales are older than Buddhism and were already folk stories across India. Some also appear in the [[@panchatantra-tales|Panchatantra]], and a few resemble the fables of [[@aesop|Aesop]], which shows how freely good stories travelled.

In the Sasa Jataka, the Bodhisatta is a hare who lives with three friends: a monkey, a jackal and an otter. They agree to give food to anyone in need. One day, the god Sakka, disguised as a hungry traveller, comes to test them. The otter brings fish, the jackal brings food it has found and the monkey brings mangoes. The hare has only grass, which a person cannot eat. So he offers himself, leaping into a fire to become a meal.

The fire doesn't burn him. Sakka, deeply moved, draws the hare's image on the [[@moon-phases|Moon]] so the world will remember his kindness. In many parts of Asia, people still look for a hare in the dark patches of the full Moon.

Over 2,000 years ago, Buddhist sculptors carved Jataka scenes on the stone railings and gateways of [[stupa|stupas]] at Bharhut and Sanchi, in [[@madhya-pradesh|Madhya Pradesh]]. Pilgrims walking around the stupa could "read" the stories in stone. Later, painters at Ajanta filled cave walls with them.

The tales spread with Buddhism to Sri Lanka, Myanmar, [[@thailand|Thailand]] and beyond. In Thailand and Laos, the Vessantara Jataka, the story of the Bodhisatta's last human life before becoming the Buddha, is recited at a festival every year. Between 1895 and 1907, scholars at Cambridge published the first complete English [[@translation|translation]], in six volumes, so readers far from India could meet the generous hare too.

text: Chewing gum has two main parts. The first is the gum base, the rubbery part that never [[dissolve|dissolves]] no matter how long you chew. The second is everything that does dissolve: sweeteners, flavours, softeners and colour.

Long ago, gum bases came from nature, such as the sticky sap of trees. Today, most gum base is made from synthetic [[polymer|polymers]], long chains of [[molecule|molecules]] similar to those in some plastics and rubbers, approved as safe to chew. Gum makers rarely share their exact recipes. The flavour fades as your [[saliva|saliva]] washes the sweeteners and flavourings away, until only the tasteless base is left.

st.prompt: Why was the first bubble gum coloured pink?

options.t: Pink was the only food colouring in the factory that day
Pink makes bubbles stronger
Scientists found that children prefer pink

st.reveal: In 1928, Walter Diemer, an accountant at a sweet company, mixed a stretchy gum that could blow bubbles. Pink food colouring was what was at hand. It stuck, and pink is still the classic bubble-gum colour.

src: Mathews J.P. and Schultz G.P., Chicle. The Chewing Gum of the Americas, From the Ancient Maya to William Wrigley. University of Arizona Press, 2009.
Encyclopaedia Britannica, Chewing gum.

d.try: Hold a stopwatch and chew a piece of sugar-free gum for one minute, then five, then ten, tasting it each time. Write down when the flavour fades. The sweeteners and flavour dissolve in your saliva and are swallowed, but the gum base, which does not dissolve, stays behind in your mouth.
myth: Swallowed chewing gum stays in your stomach for seven years.

Your body cannot digest the gum base, but it does not get stuck. It moves through your gut and leaves your body in a few days, like other things you cannot digest. Swallowing large amounts often is still a bad idea, especially for small children.
facts: birch-bark tar, thousands of years old, found in Scandinavia
chicle, sap of the sapodilla (chikoo) tree
mostly synthetic polymers, a kind of food-safe plastic

sec.t:
In Central America, the Maya and Aztecs chewed chicle, the milky sap of the sapodilla tree. Workers called chicleros climbed the trees and cut zigzag slashes into the bark, then collected the sap that oozed out and boiled it into blocks.

The sapodilla is the same tree that gives India its chikoo fruit. It was brought to India from the Americas and now grows widely in Gujarat, Maharashtra and Karnataka. Ancient Greeks had their own gum too: mastic, a resin from a tree that grows on the island of Chios.

In the 1860s, a New York inventor named Thomas Adams got a supply of chicle and tried to turn it into rubber. It did not work. Instead, he rolled it into small pieces and sold it as chewing gum, and in 1871 he patented a gum-making machine.

A salesman named William Wrigley Jr. made gum famous in the 1890s with bold advertising. Spearmint and Juicy Fruit gums, launched in 1893, are still sold. In 1928, Walter Diemer, an accountant at a Philadelphia company, found a recipe stretchy enough to [[@food-why-bubblegum-pink|blow bubbles]]. During the [[@world-war-two|Second World War]], American soldiers carried gum in their rations and helped spread it around the world.

Chicle was slow and costly to collect, and demand was huge. By the middle of the 20th century, chemists had made synthetic replacements from petroleum. Most modern gum is made from these. A few companies still sell gum made from natural chicle.

Because gum base does not break down easily, spat-out gum is a big cleaning problem. Grey blobs on pavements can stay for years, and removing them takes steam machines and scrapers.

In 1992, Singapore banned the sale of chewing gum, partly because of gum stuck on pavements and in the doors of its new metro trains. Since 2004, gum with health benefits, such as nicotine gum or some dental gums, can be sold in pharmacies. Visitors are still often surprised by the rule.

Sugar-free gum can actually help [[@teeth|teeth]]. Chewing makes more saliva, which washes away food and [[acid|acid]]. Dentists say it is no replacement for brushing, though.

text: Pani puri is a small, hollow, crisp ball of fried dough. You crack a hole in the top, fill it with potato, chickpeas or sprouts, dip it in spicy, tangy water, and pop the whole thing into your mouth at once. It's one of India's favourite street foods.

It has so many names because it spread across a country with dozens of languages and hundreds of [[@dialects|dialects]]. Each region adopted the snack and named it in its own way. In Delhi it's golgappa, in Kolkata puchka, in [[@odisha|Odisha]] gupchup, in Lucknow pani ke batashe, and in Mumbai pani puri.

st.prompt: Why does a flat disc of dough puff up into a hollow ball when it's fried?

options.t: Water in the dough turns to steam and blows it up like a balloon
Yeast in the dough grows very fast in hot oil
The oil gets inside the dough and pushes it apart

st.reveal: The thin dough holds a little water. In hot oil, that water turns to steam almost instantly. The steam pushes the two surfaces of the dough apart, and the outside crisps around a hollow middle.

src: Achaya K. T., A Historical Dictionary of Indian Food, Oxford University Press, 1998.
Google Doodles archive, "Celebrating Pani Puri" (12 July 2023).
Britannica, Indian cuisine.
n.certNote: The snack and its many names are well known. Where it first came from is unknown, and popular stories about its origin, such as the tale linking it to Draupadi, are folk tales rather than history.

d.try: Make a "name map". Ask friends, relatives or neighbours from different states what they call pani puri. Write each name on a map of India where that person grew up. See how many names you collect, and whether neighbouring states share them.
myth: Draupadi from the Mahabharata invented pani puri.

This is a popular folk tale, told as a test her mother-in-law gave her to feed five sons with very little flour. There's no historical record of where pani puri began, and the snack as we know it is probably much more recent.
facts: a hollow fried puri, a filling, and spiced water
pani puri, pakodi in parts of Gujarat

sec.t:
Each name tells a little story. "Pani puri" simply means "water puri". "Golgappa" combines "gol" (round) with "gappa", from gobbling it in one mouthful. "Gupchup" may come from the way the puri fills your mouth so you can't talk, staying "gup-chup", or quiet.

"Puchka" in Bengal may come from the crack the puri makes when it bursts. "Pani ke batashe" compares it to batasha, a light, airy sugar sweet. In parts of Gujarat, it's called pakodi, and in some places "phulki", meaning puffed.

{{story:dialects}}

These names show how food moves. A snack travels with people, but each place gives it a local name, a local filling and local water.

The puri is made from a dough of semolina, wheat flour or both. It's rolled very thin and cut into small circles. When the circles hit hot oil, the little bit of water inside the dough turns to steam in a flash.

The steam pushes the top and bottom of the circle apart, like blowing up a tiny balloon. The outside fries crisp around a hollow centre. Making perfect, evenly puffed puris takes skill, and many stalls buy them from specialist makers. It's a neat bit of [[@cooking-science|cooking science]]: water becoming gas and taking up more than a thousand times as much space.

The spiced water, or pani, is what people argue about most. A classic version blends mint, coriander, green chillies, [[@tamarind|tamarind]], black salt and roasted cumin. It's sour, spicy and sometimes very hot.

Many stalls also offer sweet water, made with tamarind and [[@jaggery|jaggery]] or dates. In Kolkata, puchka water is usually sour with tamarind, and the potato filling is mashed with chillies and spices. Mumbai stalls may offer several waters, from garlic to lemon to hing (asafoetida).

Pani puri is usually eaten standing at a cart. The seller fills one puri at a time and hands it to you on a small leaf or paper bowl. You must eat each one immediately, before it goes soggy, and the seller keeps going until you say stop.

Many sellers give a free last puri, filled only with dry stuffing and spices, called a "sukha puri". Regulars know to ask for it.

Nobody knows. A popular story says that in the [[@mahabharata|Mahabharata]], Draupadi was given leftover potatoes and a little flour, and told to feed her five husbands. She invented pani puri. It's a fun tale, but there's no historical evidence for it.

Food historians think the snack probably developed in North India in fairly recent centuries. Potatoes and chillies, now key ingredients, only reached India in the last 500 years. What we do know is that pani puri is now eaten everywhere, from village fairs to Indian restaurants in New Jersey.

text: Dal is made from pulses, the dried seeds of [[legume|legume]] plants such as [[@lentils-world|lentils]], chickpeas, pigeon peas and beans. These seeds are rich in [[protein|protein]], which your body uses to build muscles, skin and almost everything else.

Dal is also full of fibre, which keeps your [[@digestion-gut|gut]] working well, and has iron, folate and other [[nutrient|nutrients]]. Eaten with rice or roti, it makes a meal with a good balance of protein. And pulses are kind to farms too, because their roots make the soil richer.

st.prompt: Farmers often plant chana or moong between crops of wheat or rice. Why?

options.t: Their roots add nitrogen to the soil
They scare away birds from the field
They soak up extra rainwater so fields do not flood

st.reveal: Pulse plants team up with bacteria living in small lumps, called nodules, on their roots. The bacteria take nitrogen gas from the air and turn it into a form plants can use. When the pulse crop is done, the next crop gets a richer soil.

src: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), International Year of Pulses 2016.
ICMR National Institute of Nutrition, Indian Food Composition Tables (2017).
Achaya K. T. (1994) Indian Food. A Historical Companion. Oxford University Press.

d.try: Soak a handful of whole moong overnight. Drain it, wrap it in a damp cotton cloth and keep it somewhere warm. In a day or two you will see sprouts. Leave a few to grow in a cup of soil and, after some weeks, gently wash the roots to look for tiny round nodules.
myth: You need to eat meat to get enough protein.
Pulses, milk, curd, nuts and grains together can give people all the protein they need. Hundreds of millions of vegetarians in India get their protein mostly this way.
facts: World's biggest grower and eater of pulses

sec.t:
A pulse seed is a packed lunch for a baby plant. It holds the energy and building material the seedling will need before it can make its own food from sunlight. That is why dry lentils are about one fifth to one quarter protein, far more than rice or wheat.

When you eat dal, your [[@stomach-digest|stomach and gut]] break that protein into small pieces called amino [[acid|acids]]. Your body then rebuilds them into its own proteins.

sec.h: Dal and rice: a good team
sec.t:
Proteins are made from about 20 different amino acids, and the body cannot make some of them. Pulses are rich in one called lysine but low in another called methionine. Rice and wheat are the other way round.

So when you eat dal with [[@rice|rice]], or rajma with chawal, or chana with roti, the two foods fill each other's gaps. People across the world found the same answer without knowing any chemistry: beans and corn [[@tacos|tortillas]] in [[@mexico|Mexico]], and [[@peanut-butter|peanut butter]] on bread in American lunchboxes.

India grows more pulses than any other country, and eats even more, so it also buys pulses from countries such as [[@canada|Canada]], Australia and Myanmar. In the United States, the states of Montana and North Dakota grow large amounts of lentils and dry peas, much of it for [[export|export]].

Every Indian region has favourites. Toor dal goes into sambar in the south, Gujarat makes it gently sweet, and Bengal has masoor dal with fried onions. Urad dal is ground into idli batter, and chana becomes besan for pakoras.

sec.h: A seed with a long history
sec.t:
People have eaten pulses since the very beginning of farming. Lentils and chickpeas were among the first crops grown in the Fertile Crescent of West Asia, more than 10,000 years ago. Archaeologists have found charred lentils and other pulses at Harappan sites in India too.

Pulses suited early farmers well. Dried seeds are light, keep for a long time without spoiling and can be carried on long journeys. Ancient Indian texts mention mudga, which is moong, and masha, which is urad. The names have changed a little over time, but the bowl of dal has not.

Pulses have a few downsides. Some of their sugars are not digested in the stomach, so bacteria in the large intestine break them down instead and make gas. Soaking, sprouting and cooking well help, and Indian cooks add a pinch of hing, which many people believe eases it.

Raw kidney beans contain a substance that can make people sick, which is why rajma is always soaked and boiled thoroughly. Properly cooked, it is perfectly safe and very good food.
